title: Identify business success issues for SMMEs

lessons.title: What makes a small agribusiness succeed
lessons.html:
Defining success for an SMME

Success means different things to different owners. For one smallholder it is a steady income that pays school fees. For a co-operative it may be supplying a retailer every week all year. For a young entrepreneur it may be growing from 500 to 5 000 layers. As an adviser, first ask the owner what success looks like for them, then identify the issues that will make or break that goal.

Common success factors

  • A real market. Successful agribusinesses start with a buyer, not with a product. Know who will buy, how much, how often, at what price and to what standard.
  • Sound financial management. Separating business and household money, keeping records, budgeting and managing cash flow.
  • Technical competence. Knowing how to produce efficiently: correct planting dates, vaccination programmes, feeding, irrigation scheduling.
  • Management and leadership. Clear decision-making, planning ahead, and the ability to manage workers and relationships.
  • Access to resources. Secure land tenure, reliable water, finance, inputs and transport.
  • Personal qualities of the owner. Commitment, resilience, willingness to learn and take calculated risks.

Research on small business across many countries shows that owner capability and market access are among the strongest predictors of survival. In South African agriculture, secure tenure and reliable water are also critical, because without them a farmer cannot invest or borrow.

Thinking in systems

These factors are connected. A vegetable grower with a good market but no cold storage or transport may lose produce. A broiler farmer with excellent technical skills but poor cash management may fail to buy feed for the next batch. Your task is to look at the whole system and find the weakest link.

lessons.title: Common causes of SMME failure in agriculture
lessons.html:
Learning from failure

Many emerging farmer projects in South Africa have failed despite grants and support. Understanding why helps you spot warning signs early.

Typical causes

CauseExample
Production before marketA group plants five hectares of butternut with no buyer and sells at a loss on the roadside.
Poor cash flow managementGrant money is spent on infrastructure, leaving no working capital for feed or seed.
Mixing household and business moneySales income is used for family needs, so inputs cannot be bought on time.
Weak group governanceCo-operative members disagree over profits, attendance drops and the project collapses.
Over-reliance on one buyer or one productA single contract ends and the business has no other outlet.
Unmanaged riskNo plan for drought, disease outbreaks, stock theft or equipment breakdown.
Non-complianceLack of registration, tax compliance or required certification blocks access to formal markets.

Warning signs

Watch for late payment of suppliers, increasing debt, falling production records, staff leaving, key members missing meetings, and an owner who avoids discussing finances. Early warning allows corrective action before the business fails.

External factors matter too: input price increases, interest rates, exchange rates affecting fertiliser and fuel costs, load shedding affecting irrigation and cold rooms, and poor rural roads. An SMME cannot control these, but it can plan for them, for example by budgeting conservatively, keeping a cash reserve, installing backup power where viable, or joining with other farmers to buy inputs in bulk.

When advising, be honest. Pointing out a serious weakness early is more helpful than polite encouragement that ends in failure.

lessons.title: Assessing and prioritising success issues
lessons.html:
A structured assessment

To identify success issues for a particular SMME, work through a structured assessment with the owner. A useful approach is to score each success factor, for example from 1 (very weak) to 5 (very strong), using evidence rather than impressions.

  1. List the factors: market, finance, production, management, resources, compliance and owner capability.
  2. Gather evidence: sales records, buyer agreements, bank statements, production records, interviews and site observation.
  3. Score jointly: discuss each score with the owner so they understand and agree.
  4. Identify the critical few: select the two or three weakest factors that most limit success.
  5. Look for root causes: ask why repeatedly. Low egg sales may be due to poor quality, which may be due to poor feed, which may be due to cash shortages at the time of purchase.

Prioritising

Not all issues are equally urgent. Use two questions: how big is the impact on the business, and how easily can it be fixed? Issues with high impact that can be fixed quickly, such as starting a simple cash book or negotiating a written supply agreement, should be tackled first. High-impact issues that take longer, such as securing a long-term lease, need a planned approach and often support from other role players.

Agreeing actions

For each priority issue, agree specific actions, who is responsible, the timeframe and the support needed, such as mentoring, a short course, a referral to a financier, or a meeting with a buyer. Follow up regularly to check progress. Success issues change as the business grows, so repeat the assessment once or twice a year.

Key points

  • Start by asking what success means to the owner.
  • Market access, financial management, technical skill, management, resources and owner capability drive success.
  • Common failures include producing before finding a market and running out of working capital.
  • Score success factors with evidence and find root causes.
  • Prioritise issues by impact and ease of fixing, and agree specific actions.
